goal: Deliver working sign-in for the internal admin-panel app and settle how authenticated state is carried between requests so the five-person team can implement it.
question: Select the authentication state strategy that best matches the current admin-panel project.
known_constraints: Python standard library only; the repository has no dependency manifest and no web framework.
The app is server-rendered HTML served from a single origin by its own web server.
The app is an internal tool for a five-person team with no external API consumers today.
A possible mobile app appears on the product roadmap but nothing has been decided.
evidence: app.py is described as a 'Minimal server-rendered admin panel (stdlib only)' and uses http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler with a single do_GET handler and no POST, cookie, session, or token handling (app.py).
The served page already contains a sign-in form placeholder: <form action='/login'>sign-in form</form> (app.py).
The server runs as a single process bound to 127.0.0.1:8080 (app.py).
The README describes an internal admin panel for a five-person team, server-rendered by its own web server, served from a single origin, with no external API consumers today (README.md).
The README notes the product roadmap mentions a possible mobile app, but nothing has been decided (README.md).

The repository contains only app.py and README.md plus configuration; there is no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or other dependency manifest, so no third-party auth libraries are present (repository tree).

alternatives.name: Server-side session with HttpOnly cookie
alternatives.description: Issue an opaque session ID at login, keep the session state server-side, and return it as an HttpOnly Set-Cookie that the browser sends back on each request.
advantages: Session state lives server-side, so access can be revoked immediately by deleting the session record.
An HttpOnly cookie is not readable by page JavaScript, which limits token theft through XSS.
Browsers attach cookies automatically on the same origin, so no client-side code is needed in the server-rendered pages.
Fits the stdlib-only constraint: a cookie header and an in-memory dict are sufficient for five users.
disadvantages: A session store must exist server-side; an in-memory store is per-process and is lost on restart unless persisted.
Native mobile apps and non-browser clients need additional handling to persist and send the cookie.
assumptions: The admin panel remains browser-accessed and same-origin.
A per-process or file-backed session store is acceptable for five users.

alternatives.name: Stateless signed bearer token (JWT-style)
alternatives.description: Issue a self-contained signed token at login that the client stores and presents as an Authorization: Bearer header on each request, so verification needs no server-side session store.
advantages: No server-side session storage; each request is verified from the token signature alone.
The same verification path serves any client type, including a future mobile app or API consumers.
disadvantages: The client must hold the token in JavaScript-accessible storage and attach headers manually, which the current server-rendered form flow does not do.
Revoking a token before expiry requires additional deny-list machinery.
Expiry handling and signing-secret management add moving parts on top of the stdlib hmac primitives.
assumptions: Clients are able to store tokens and attach Authorization headers.
Non-browser client reuse is a real near-term requirement rather than a speculative roadmap item.

alternatives.name: HTTP Basic authentication (no stored login state)
alternatives.description: Protect routes with HTTP Basic so credentials are supplied on every request and no login state is stored or issued at all.
advantages: No session store, expiry, or revocation logic to build; stdlib Base64 decoding is sufficient.
Works identically for browsers, curl, and any future client because credentials travel with each request.
disadvantages: Credentials are transmitted on every request and there is no logout action or session expiry.
Browsers show a native, non-customizable prompt, which does not match the sign-in form the current page already sketches.
Password entry and transmission are repeated per request rather than exchanged once for a short-lived credential.
assumptions: Team members accept the browser's native Basic-auth prompt in place of a form-based sign-in.

criteria.name: Same-origin browser fit
rubric: Requires client-side storage and manual header handling in the browser
Usable in browsers with extra setup or code
Browser-native: automatic transport with no client-side code

criteria.name: Stdlib-only feasibility
rubric: Requires external dependencies or significant crypto/state machinery
Implementable with the stdlib but with several moving parts
Implementable with stdlib primitives in a small amount of code

criteria.name: Logout and revocation lifecycle
rubric: No logout or revocation path exists
Revocation requires additional machinery to build
Immediate revocation by deleting server-side state

criteria.name: Roadmap flexibility (possible mobile app)
rubric: Browser-only transport; new client types need a parallel mechanism
Works for non-browser clients with extra client-side handling
Transport-neutral across browser and non-browser clients

criteria.name: Operational risk for a five-person internal team
rubric: Multiple new secrets or stores to operate, or credentials sent on every request
One new component to operate (session store or signing secret)
No additional state or secrets beyond existing user credentials
